lawyer:
Md. Abdur Rashid, Advocate ----- for the Petitioner 
Kazi Ebadul Haque, Advocate ----- for the Opposite party
parties:
Anwara Begum
Vs.
Maimuna Khatun Chowdhury & Other
full_judgment:
A. T. M. Afzal J:- These three Rules at the instance of the pre-emptee-petitioner are directed against orders allowing pre-emption under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act 1950, hereinafter called the Act, passed by the learned Munsif, 2nd Court, Feni, in Misc, case Nos. 217,218 and 219 of 1973 and confirmed in appeal (Misc. appeals Nos. 56,57 and 58 of 1976) by the District Judge, Noakhali on 5.1.78. 

 2. The opposite party No. 1 Maimuna Khatun Chowdhury instituted the aforesaid cases for obtaining pre-emption under section 96 of the Act in respect of 18 decimals, 30 decimals and '6 decimals of lands respectively appertaining to plot No. 247 under khatian No. 92 (S.A. Khatian No. 115) of mouse Mohammadpur, P.S. Feni, District Noakhali. Her case was that her father Abdul Jabbar Chowdhury was a co-sharer in the holding in question by purchase. He died leaving two sons Fazlul Karim and Bazlul Karim Chowdury and two daughters Umme Salema and Maimuna Khatun (pre-emptor 0,P, No, 1). Her brother Fazlul Karim Chowdhury sold '18 decimals of land to the petitioner by kabala dated 30.1.71 for Tk. 1000/-, both of her brothers also sold '30 decimals of land to the petitioner by kabala dated 1.4.70 for a consideration of Tk. 2000/- and again her brother Bazlul Karim alone sold '6 decimals of land to the petitioner by kabala dated 16.6.72 for a consideration of Tk. 500/-. The opposite party No. 1 alleged that the petitioner was a stranger to the holding and that on notice of the aforesaid transfers was served on her. She stated that she purchased the share of her sister Umme Salma by kabala dated 21.7.73. After her purchase she went to possess the land and at that time came to know about the purchases made by the petitioner from her brothers. She came to know about the transfers on 14.8.73 and upon obtaining certified copies of the kabalas in question filed the Misc, cases on 30.8.73. 

 9. It was found by the learned District Judge that the pre-emptor-O.P. No. I was a non-notified co-sharer. Her case was that she purchased the share of her sister Unune Salma by kabala dated 21-7-73 Ext. 1(Ga) and that when she went to her father's house in village Mohammadpur on 14.8.73 to possess her purchased land she came to know of the transfers made by her brothers to the petitioner. She was corroborated by her son P.W. 2. The learned District Judge upon a consideration of the oral evidence and the circumstances of the case, particularly the strained relationship between the pre-emptor and her brothers came to the conclusion that there was no reason to disbelieve her (pre-emptor's) case regarding the date of knowledge. The learned Advocate for the petitioner has argued that the evidence of the O.P. No. 1 was vague in that she did not state from whom she had learnt about the transfers. The allegation seem to be unfounded because the O.P. No. 1 clearly stated in cross-examination that she had learnt about the transfers from her son and other persons. The learned Advocate has then argued that the courts below ought to have drawn a presumption adverse to the pre-emptor for not examining one Moklesur Rahman and Saleh Ahmed from whom P.W. 2 was alleged to have learnt about the transfers. The learned Advocate has sought to reinforce his submission by referring to a decision reported in 1981 BLD 56. In that case the evidence as to the date of knowledge was given by the pre-emptor alone and the courts below accepted his evidence. But in this court it was observed that since the pre-emptor's son, who was allegedly present when the knowledge of the transfer occurred, was not examined and no explanation was given for his non-examination, the courts below failed to exercise their jurisdiction in not drawing an adverse presumption on that account and further that the pre-emptor had 'failed to prove the date of his knowledge and as such the application was barred by limitation. With respect, I would like to observe that I do not find any aspect of jurisdiction being involved in the alleged failure of the courts below to draw an ad-'verse presumption as held in the case cited and contended by the learned Advocate. Moreover, the facts of the case referred to are entirely different from that of the present case. In the instant case the evidence of the pre-emptor was corroborated by that of her son P.W 2. The District Judge also referred to the circumstances of the case while assessing the evidence of the O.P. No. 1 on the point. Moreover, there could not be any question of examining Moklesur Rahman and others by the O.P. No. 1 because these were the persons who were said to have resisted the preemptor's son from possessing the land in question pursuant to her purchase from Umme Salma. Having regard to the evidence on record and the findings of the courts below arrived at upon a proper consideration there-of I am not at all impressed by the submission of the learned Advocate for the petitioner which is accordingly rejected. 

 11. It is true that neither of the courts below recorded any finding as aforesaid. In the instant cases, the pre-emptor clearly stated in her applications that there would be no violation of P.O. 98 of 1972 if pre-emption was allowed in her favour. There was no denial to this statement given by the petitioner. The pre-emptor in her evidence also clearly stated that she had only 8/9 bighas of land. Therefore, in solar as the onus upon the pre-emptor was there it was fully discharged. In the case cited by the learned Advocate the facts were similar and it was held that the pre-emptor having discharged her onus it was the duty of the court to record a finding in terms of the proviso to section 96(1) of the Act. His Lordship further held that if there was no such finding the application for pre-emption was bound to fail. With great respect, I do not see why the application for pre-emption must fail in such circumstances. It has been observed by his Lordship in that case that the embargo contained in the proviso to section 96(1) of the Act, if overlooked, shall render section 90(1) of the Act nugatory. It is apparent that the 'embargo' referred to was in fact not there either in that case or in the cases under consideration. What was not there was merely a finding of the court in that behalf for which the party could not be penalized. If the courts below failed to determine a material issue in spite of necessary pleadings and evidence, this court would certainly direct in the exercise of its revisional jurisdiction to determine the issue and to record necessary finding. I am not aware of any principle on which a party to a suit or proceeding should be made to suffer or a right be made infructuous for the failure of the court to do its duty. If there is such a failure this court can and shall always correct such lapse and thus prevent a right of a party from being frustrated on that account. In the facts of the present cases and even in those of the case referred to above the trial court had no option but to hold that the order allowing pre-emption would not offend section 90 of the Act. In the circumstances of the case, however, I do not consider it proper to make an order of remand for recording the said finding for this court can itself record the finding when there is no dispute whatsoever on the point and the pleadings and the evidence are complete. On the basis of undisputed fact I hold that the pre-emptor is a person who is entitled to purchase under section 96 of the Act and to whom transfer as sought for could be made under section 90 of the Act. In such view of the matter the second submission of the learned Advocate for the petitioner also falls through. Lastly, Mr. Rashid has argued that the courts below acted illegally and with material irregularity is not considering that the petitioner was a co-sharer herself by purchase and as such entitled to proportionate pre-emption. Having gone through the judgments of the courts below it is found that neither of the courts gave any consideration to the petitioner's assertion for whatever it was worth that she was also a co-sharer by purchase. She dearly set out such a case in her written objections and also led evidence to show that by kabala dated 5.9.70 she became a co-sharer in the holding in question. Now let us examine as to whether this non-consideration by the courts below has affected the decision on the merits. The pre-emptor has claimed pre-emption as a co-sharer in the holding by inheritance. It is found from the khatian No. 115 Ext. 2(Ka) that the pre-emptor along with her brothers and sister are the recorded tenants as heirs of Abdul Jabbar Chowdhury. Therefore, as between the pre-emptor and the pre-emptee-petitioner the former had a prior right to purchase under sub-section (5) of section 96 of the Act. Even if the petitioner was a co-sharer by purchase which has been disputed in the counter-affidavit filed by the O.P. No. 1 and to which my reply has been given, the fact remains that the pre-emptor would have a prior right vis-a-vis the petitioner and in such view of the matter the results in the cases are not affected in the least for the alleged non-consideration of the status of the petitioner by the courts below.
